title: Equity as residual claim
body: Common equity is a residual claim: after creditors, preferred holders, and other senior claims are satisfied, shareholders own what remains of firm value. That residual can compound handsomely in good states — or go to zero in distress — which is why equity expected returns and volatility sit above senior debt. Thinking in priority of claims clarifies capital structure, recovery, and why leverage amplifies equity outcomes. In underwriting and recovery analysis, map the full priority stack before estimating equity upside: guarantees, preferred, leases, and pensions can sit ahead of common. Leverage changes how asset outcomes are sliced, which is why the same enterprise shock produces asymmetric equity paths.
example: Firm assets mark at $100. Senior debt is $70. Equity’s residual claim is $30. If assets fall to $60 in a downturn, debt still claims $60 (subject to recovery frictions) and equity is wiped — a −100% equity outcome on a −40% asset move. Step through: assets $100 → equity cushion $30. Assets −40% to $60: senior debt still covers from remaining value, equity → $0. Equity return = −100% while asset return = −40%; the difference is leverage through priority, not a separate equity-market shock.
eli5: Imagine a lemonade stand that must pay its helper and its loan first. The owner only gets what is left — which can grow when business is great, or be nothing when it is not.

title: Fixed income cash flows
body: A vanilla bond is a contractual schedule: periodic coupons plus principal at maturity, priced by discounting each cash flow at rates that embed credit, liquidity, and the yield curve. When discount rates rise, present value falls — the classic inverse price–yield relationship. Everything else (duration, spreads, call risk) is a refinement of that cash-flow machine. Desks still start from the contractual schedule even for spread products: once cash-flow dates and amounts are fixed, everything else is discounting and optionality. Accrued interest, day-count, and settlement conventions change dirty vs clean price on real tickets.
example: A 2-year 5% annual coupon bond with $100 face pays $5 then $105. At a flat 5% discount rate, price ≈ $100. If the discount rate jumps to 6%, price ≈ $98.17 — about a 1.8% mark-to-market loss before any credit news. Cash flows: +5 at t=1, +105 at t=2. PV at 5%: 5/1.05 + 105/1.05² = 100. At 6%: 5/1.06 + 105/1.06² ≈ 4.717 + 93.450 = 98.17. Price change ≈ −1.83% from a +100 bp flat discount-rate shock alone.
eli5: A bond is a written IOU: small thank-you payments along the way, then the loan back at the end. If newer safer loans suddenly pay more, your older IOU is worth a bit less.

title: Commodities vs financial assets
body: Most commodities pay no coupon or dividend. Returns come from spot moves, futures roll yield along the curve, and sometimes convenience yield for holders of inventory. Physical ownership also burns storage, insurance, and financing — costs financial claims do not share. Treat commodity beta as a different engine than equity or credit. A commodity position is an inventory and curve problem as much as a directional bet. Convenience yield, storage, and roll dominate multi-month holding-period returns; treating futures like equity without dividends mis-states both carry and risk.
example: You are long a futures curve in 2% annual contango. Ignoring spot drift, rolling the front contract each month leaks roughly ~2% per year in roll yield — so the futures P&L can lag the spot narrative by that bleed. If the curve’s annualized contango is ~2% and spot is unchanged, each roll roughly monetizes that slope against the long. Over a year of monthly rolls, expect on the order of ~2% drag before spot P&L — futures return ≠ spot headline.
eli5: A barrel of oil does not mail you interest, and storing it costs money. Futures can gain or lose from the shape of future prices even when today’s warehouse price barely moves.

title: FX as a relative price
body: An FX rate is the relative price of two currencies (two monetary and fiscal regimes). Spot FX alone has no coupon; carry and risk premia appear when you fund one currency with another or hedge with forwards. Every unhedged foreign asset is an asset view plus an FX view. FX embeds relative monetary policy, growth, and risk appetite. Unhedged foreign assets always carry an FX overlay; the only choice is whether that overlay is intentional, sized, and financed.
example: USD/JPY at 150 means ¥150 per $1. A U.S. investor holding ¥10,000,000 of Japanese equities has equity risk plus FX risk: a move to 160 (dollar stronger) cuts dollar value of the same yen shares by ~6.25% even if local prices are flat. ¥10,000,000 / 150 = $66,667. At 160: ¥10,000,000 / 160 = $62,500. FX translation P&L ≈ −$4,167 (−6.25%) with local equity flat — an FX overlay equal to a mid-single-digit equity move.
eli5: An exchange rate is how many blue tickets trade for one red ticket. Your overseas shop can do fine and you still earn less at home if the tickets trade differently.

title: Alternatives umbrella
body: ‘Alternatives’ bundles private equity, hedge funds, real assets, infrastructure, and private credit — strategies that often trade liquidity, transparency, and fees for different return drivers and lower day-to-day mark correlation. The label is not a risk free lunch; it is a structural choice about how and when risk is observed. The alternatives label hides very different liquidity clocks and fee stacks. Underwrite redemption terms, valuation policy, and leverage separately — a low reported correlation often reflects stale marks more than true diversification.
example: A $10m commitment to a PE fund may show ~flat marks in year 1 while fees and capital calls run, then jump on an exit in year 5. Same economic risk, very different reported path than a daily-liquidity equity sleeve of equal size. Year 0–1: capital calls and fees can leave NAV below contributed capital even if deals are fine. Year 5 exit may jump TVPI in one mark. Compare that path to a $10m liquid equity sleeve marked daily — same capital, different observability of risk.
eli5: “Alternatives” is a big box for investments that do not price every day like ordinary shares. Calmer reported numbers can mean slower selling — not that nothing bad can happen.

title: Primary vs secondary markets
body: Primary markets raise capital (IPOs, bond syndications, private placements). Secondary markets transfer existing claims between investors. Issuers receive cash only in the primary; secondary prices still matter because they set the opportunity cost of future issuance and the mark for holders. Primary clearing levels set the issuer’s cost of capital; secondary marks set holders’ opportunity cost and the reference for the next deal. Confusing “we raised at par” with “the bond is still worth par” drifts from portfolio reality.
example: Company issues $500m of bonds at par in the primary. A week later the bonds trade at 98 in the secondary. The issuer already has its $500m; existing holders mark a ~2% loss, and the next issue will price off that secondary clearing level. Primary: issuer receives ~$500m. Secondary at 98: holders mark −2 points (~$10m on $500m face). Next issue prices off ~98, not the prior par print — secondary discovery set the new cost of capital.
eli5: Primary is when a company first sells new tickets for cash. Secondary is fans trading those tickets with each other — the company does not get that later cash.

title: Exchange vs OTC
body: Exchanges standardize contracts, concentrate liquidity, and usually clear through a CCP. OTC markets customize terms bilaterally — more flexible, but you inherit counterparty, documentation, and often less transparent pricing. Same economic hedge can be a listed future or an OTC forward with very different ops and risk plumbing. Choose venue for the risk you want to warehouse: standardization and CCP margin versus customization and bilateral CSA terms. Ops capacity, documentation, and stress liquidity often matter more than a few basis points of mid-market edge.
example: Hedging $50m of rate risk with a listed Treasury future uses exchange margin and daily variation margin. The same DV01 via an OTC swap needs an ISDA, CSA collateral terms, and bilateral (or cleared) counterparty management — different ops even if the macro view matches. Listed future: initial margin + daily VM. OTC swap: ISDA/CSA, possible thresholds, and bilateral call timing. Same ~DV01 can demand different cash calendars; ops and liquidity planning follow the wrapper.
eli5: An exchange is a shared playground with standard rules and a referee. OTC is a custom handshake between two sides — flexible, but you must trust and paper the handshake.

title: Central clearing
body: A CCP novates trades: it becomes buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. Counterparty risk is mutualized through margin and default funds rather than eliminated. Clearing concentrates risk in a supervised node — resilient by design, systemic if that node is mismanaged. Clearing mutualizes default risk and standardizes variation margin, but concentrates operational and liquidity dependence on the CCP and its members. Initial margin models and default-fund sizing are first-order risk parameters.
example: A and B trade a swap. After novation, A faces the CCP and B faces the CCP — not each other. If B defaults, the CCP uses B’s margin and mutualized resources; A’s replacement risk is to the clearinghouse process, not B’s bankruptcy estate directly. Pre-novation A↔B; post-novation A↔CCP and B↔CCP. B’s default: CCP waterfalls B’s IM/VM and mutualized resources. A faces CCP processes — not B’s bankruptcy estate directly — for replacement.
eli5: A clearinghouse stands in the middle so you are not relying on the other kid directly. Risk is shared with safety deposits — concentrated in one careful middle player.

title: Order books and spreads
body: The bid–ask spread compensates liquidity providers for inventory risk and adverse selection. Tight spreads signal competitive liquidity; wide spreads flag uncertainty, thin books, or informed flow. Last trade is a point sample; the book is the cost of actually trading. Spread and depth jointly price adverse selection and inventory risk. A tight top-of-book with hollow size is not the same market as a one-tick market with real depth — impact lives in the levels you walk.
example: Stock shows last trade $100.00. Best bid $99.90 / best ask $100.10 (10¢ spread). Buying 1 share costs $100.10; the round-trip bid–ask tax on a tiny clip is 20¢ (~0.2%). Walking a thin book for 50,000 shares costs far more than that top-of-book print. Buy 1 at 100.10, sell 1 at 99.90 → round-trip 0.20 on ~100 = 0.20%. For 50,000 shares, if size beyond top clips deeper asks, average buy price may be 100.25+ — impact dominates the 10¢ spread narrative.
eli5: The buy pile and sell pile disagree a little; that gap is the spread. Crossing it is the small toll for trading right now instead of waiting.

title: Price discovery
body: Price discovery is how trading aggregates dispersed information into a quote. Illiquid or fragmented venues do not lack a price — they have noisier, slower discovery and larger gaps between prints. Policy and microstructure reforms often aim at discovery quality, not just average volume. Discovery quality is about how quickly and cleanly dispersed information enters tradable quotes. Fragmentation, odd-lot prints, and delayed opens create prices that are poor anchors for marking large risk.
example: A small-cap prints $12.00 on 200 shares, then $12.40 on 5,000 shares after a research note. The ‘price’ moved 3.3%, but discovery was a sequence of thin prints — using the first print as a fair-value anchor for a block trade would misstate impact. First print $12.00 × 200 is a weak fair-value signal. Later $12.40 × 5,000 after information is a more informative discovery step. Anchoring a block at $12.00 would misstate both mid and impact.
eli5: Price discovery is how many small trades teach everyone what something is worth. Thin markets learn slowly and can jump when a bigger trade finally arrives.

title: Dark pools
body: Dark pools match orders without displaying depth pre-trade, mainly to reduce signaling for large institutional size. The trade-off is less pre-trade transparency and potential fragmentation of lit liquidity. They are a tool for minimizing information leakage, not a separate asset class. Dark venues trade pre-trade transparency for reduced signaling. Fill uncertainty and potential information leakage to other users are the costs; they are execution tools, not alpha sources by themselves.
example: A fund needs to sell 2% of ADV in a name. Showing that size on the lit book can push the offer down before the order finishes. Routing slices to a dark pool aims to fill closer to mid with less displayed signal — at the cost of uncertain fill probability. 2% of ADV sold entirely on lit display can walk the book and signal. Slicing into dark mid aims for less information leakage; measure opportunity cost of partial fills if the lit print runs away.
eli5: A dark pool is a quiet trading room where big orders try not to tip off the crowd. You may hide better — but you are less sure you will finish the trade.

title: Settlement vs trading
body: Trade date is when you agree; settlement is when cash and securities actually exchange (often T+1 for equities). Settlement risk, fails, and custodian pipelines matter as much as the screen price for real balance-sheet outcomes. Economic exposure starts on trade date; legally final ownership and cash move on settlement. Fails, holidays, and cut-offs create funding and securities-lending consequences even when screen P&L looks clean.
example: You buy shares on Monday (T). Under T+1, cash and stock exchange Tuesday. If you mark the position Monday night you already have price risk, but funding and securities ownership finalize on settlement — fails or holiday calendars can still delay that final exchange. Monday trade: Tuesday settle under T+1. Monday night mark already embeds price risk; cash funding and stock delivery finalize Tuesday. A fail turns a done trade into a financing/securities problem.
eli5: Saying “deal!” is trade date; actually swapping the toy and the money is settlement. Until settlement finishes, paperwork and timing can still get messy.

title: Discounted cash flow
body: DCF says value equals expected future cash flows discounted for time and risk. The algebra is simple; the craft is honest forecasts, a coherent discount rate, and humility about terminal-value dominance. Precision past the decimal usually overstates knowledge. A DCF is only as honest as its cash-flow definition, risk-adjusted discount rate, and terminal-value story. Near-term forecast precision rarely offsets a poorly challenged exit multiple or perpetual growth rate.
example: Project pays $10 next year and $10 the year after, then zero. At a 10% discount rate, PV = 10/1.1 + 10/1.1² ≈ $17.36. Raise the discount rate to 12% and PV ≈ $16.83 — a ~3% value change from a 200 bp rate assumption shift alone. PV₀ = 10/1.10 + 10/1.21 = 9.091 + 8.264 = 17.355. At 12%: 10/1.12 + 10/1.2544 ≈ 8.929 + 7.972 = 16.901. ΔV ≈ −2.6% from +200 bp discount rate with cash flows fixed.
eli5: A cookie tomorrow is nice, but not as nice as a cookie today. DCF adds up future cookies after making them smaller for waiting and for doubt.

title: Enterprise vs equity value
body: Enterprise value (EV) is the value of core operations to all capital providers. Equity value ≈ EV − net debt (and similar claims). Mixing EV multiples with equity metrics (or ignoring net cash) is a classic way to mis-compare levered and unlevered firms. Always reconcile EV to equity through net debt and other claims before comparing multiples. Mixing EV/EBITDA with P/E across different leverage is a category error that survives in too many decks.
example: EV = $800m, net debt = $300m ⇒ equity value = $500m. At 50m shares, equity value implies $10/share. An ‘EV/EBITDA of 8×’ is not comparable to a ‘P/E of 8×’ without translating claims and earnings definitions. Equity bridge: 800 − 300 = 500; per share 500/50 = 10. If someone quotes 8× without saying EV or equity and without matching the earnings definition, the comparison is undefined.
eli5: Think of a house with a mortgage: the house price is the whole business, and the owner’s part is what is left after the mortgage.

title: Multiples are abbreviated DCFs
body: Trading multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA) compress growth, margins, risk, and capital intensity into one ratio. A ‘cheap’ multiple can be mispricing — or correctly priced low growth, high leverage, or poor earnings quality. Always ask which DCF assumptions the multiple embeds. Back out the growth, margin, and reinvestment path a multiple implies before calling something cheap. Identical P/Es can embed very different IRRs once capital intensity and fade rates differ.
example: Two firms print 10× forward EPS. Firm A grows EPS 15% with light capex; Firm B grows 2% with heavy reinvestment. Same multiple, very different implied IRRs once you unpack the growth and reinvestment story behind the abbreviation. Same 10× forward EPS: A’s faster growth and lighter reinvestment imply a higher justified multiple in a DCF fade model; B’s low growth/high reinvestment implies a lower one. Equal multiples ≠ equal expected IRRs.
eli5: A price multiple is a shortcut for a long story about growth and risk. Two shops with the same shortcut can still have very different futures.

title: Cost of capital
body: WACC blends after-tax cost of debt and cost of equity at target weights. Using yesterday’s capital structure for tomorrow’s project, or discounting equity cash flows at WACC, quietly breaks the model. Match the discount rate to the cash-flow claim. Match the rate to the claim: WACC for free cash flow to firm, cost of equity for levered equity cash flows. Using target weights for a project that changes leverage quietly biases NPV.
example: Target weights 40% debt / 60% equity. Cost of debt 5% (tax 25% ⇒ after-tax 3.75%), cost of equity 10%. WACC = 0.4×3.75% + 0.6×10% = 7.5%. Discounting levered equity free cash flows at 7.5% (instead of 10%) double-counts the debt benefit. After-tax debt 5%×(1−0.25)=3.75%. WACC=0.4×3.75%+0.6×10%=7.5%. Equity FCF should use ~10%, not 7.5%; using WACC on equity cash flows understates required return and overstates value.
eli5: A project should earn more than it costs to borrow money and to keep owners happy. That hurdle rate is the cost of capital.

title: Risk-free rate building block
body: The risk-free rate anchors discount rates. Desks typically use government yields matching cash-flow currency and horizon, then layer credit, equity, and liquidity premia. Currency mismatch here is a silent valuation bug. Pick the government curve in the cash-flow currency and roughly matching horizon, then add premia explicitly. Mixing USD Treasuries into a EUR valuation embeds an FX and rate error before any ERP debate.
example: Valuing EUR cash flows with a USD Treasury 10y as ‘risk-free’ ignores EUR rate levels and FX. If German 10y is 2.5% and UST 10y is 4.0%, using 4% as the EUR risk-free base overstates the discount rate before any equity premium is added. Using 4.0% UST as EUR rf when local govies are 2.5% adds 150 bp of erroneous discounting before ERP. Correct base ≈ 2.5% (currency-matched), then add EUR equity/credit premia.
eli5: Start with the safest loan in the same kind of money and time period, then add extra for risk. Using the wrong country’s safe rate quietly breaks the recipe.

title: Terminal value dominance
body: In many DCFs, most of the value sits in the terminal value. Small changes in long-run growth or exit multiple dwarf year-1–5 forecast precision. Stress the terminal assumptions harder than the near-term spreadsheet cosmetics. If terminal value is most of EV, stress growth, fade, and exit multiple harder than year-2 margin tweaks. A tidy five-year model with an unexamined perpetuity is precision theatre, not a valuation.
example: Explicit forecast PV = $40. Terminal value PV = $160 (80% of total $200). Cutting the perpetual growth rate from 3% to 2% might drop terminal PV to ~$130, wiping ~$30 (~15%) of firm value while ‘years 1–5’ barely move. If TV PV falls 160→130 (−30) on a 3%→2% g cut, total value 200→170 (−15%). Explicit period unchanged — terminal assumptions dominated the valuation risk.
eli5: In many price guesses, most of the value is “everything after year five.” Changing that far-away assumption can matter more than tiny tweaks to next year.

title: Risk and expected return
body: In equilibrium models, higher systematic risk should earn higher expected return. Realized return is noisy; expected return is what the market prices ex ante. Conflating a lucky path with a priced risk premium is how backtests become marketing. Expected return is an ex-ante price of risk; realized return is one noisy draw. Short-sample underperformance rarely falsifies a premium — but it does test whether the investor can hold through the path.
example: Asset priced for 8% expected return with 15% vol. Over one year it returns −5%. That realization does not prove the ex-ante premium was wrong — one draw from a wide distribution. Ten years of underperformance is a harder signal; one year is mostly noise. Ex-ante E[r]=8%, σ=15%. One-year −5% is ~−0.87σ from mean — common noise, not proof the premium was zero. Evaluate premia on long samples and economic plausibility, not one print.
eli5: Being paid for risk is about what people expect going in. One unlucky year does not prove the pay was never real — it may just be a bumpy path.

title: Idiosyncratic vs systematic risk
body: Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified in a broad portfolio; systematic risk cannot. CAPM-style pricing cares about non-diversifiable exposure. Concentrated stock pickers bear both — and need compensation (or skill) for the diversifiable slice markets do not have to pay. Diversifiable risk need not earn a premium in equilibrium models; concentrated holders still feel it. Know whether you are being paid for beta or for residual volatility you could have diversified away.
example: A single stock has 40% vol; half is idiosyncratic. In a 50-stock equal-weight book of similar names with low residual correlation, idiosyncratic vol shrinks toward ~40%/√50 ≈ 5.7%, while market beta risk remains. Single-name vol 40% with half idiosyncratic ≈ 20% residual. In N=50 equal-weight, low-corr residuals, residual vol scales ~20%/√50 ≈ 2.8% contribution order of magnitude — market beta remains.
eli5: Some bumps are unique to one shop and shrink in a big mix. Market-wide bumps do not shrink that way — everyone feels them together.

title: Volatility is not the only risk
topic: Volatility is not the only risk
body: Standard deviation treats upside and downside symmetrically and ignores liquidity, path dependence, and drawdown pain. A strategy can look low-vol until the left tail arrives. Risk management needs more than a single second-moment summary. Vol ignores skew, liquidity gaps, and path-dependent funding stress. Low historical vol strategies that sell tails can look safe until the month the second moment never priced.
example: Strategy A: +1% most months, −20% in crashes, historical vol 8%. Strategy B: ±3% monthly noise, vol 10%, shallow drawdowns. A vol-only screen prefers A — until the crash month that vol averages had down-weighted. Strategy A’s rare −20% month can dominate lifetime utility despite 8% vol. Compare max drawdown, liquidity, and gap risk — not only annualized σ — before preferring A over noisier B.
eli5: A smooth ride most days can still hide one nasty surprise. “Not very bumpy on average” is not the same as “safe in a storm.”

title: Diversification math
body: Portfolio variance depends on weighted variances and covariances. Adding a volatile asset can still reduce portfolio risk if correlation is low enough. Diversification fails when correlations spike in stress — precisely when you wanted the hedge. Covariance, not average vol, drives portfolio risk. Correlation regime shifts in stress are the usual way a diversified book suddenly behaves like one bet.
example: Two assets, each 20% vol, equal weight. If correlation = 0, portfolio vol ≈ 14.1%. If correlation rises to 1 in a crisis, portfolio vol = 20%. Same weights, very different risk when the correlation regime shifts. Equal-weight two assets, σ=20%: σ_p = 20%×√((1+ρ)/2). ρ=0 → ~14.1%; ρ=1 → 20%. Crisis ρ spike erases most diversification benefit without changing weights.
eli5: A picnic is safer with several foods than with one that might spoil. Helpers help most when they do not all fail on the same rainy day.

title: Efficient frontier
body: Mean–variance optimization maps portfolios that maximize expected return for a given variance. Estimated inputs are noisy, so unconstrained ‘optimal’ weights often concentrate and churn. Regularization and constraints are part of professional practice, not optional extras. Mean–variance frontiers amplify estimation error; unconstrained optima often concentrate in the noisiest expected-return inputs. Constraints and resampling are part of professional practice.
example: Optimizer sees Asset X expected return 12% vs 8% for Y, similar vol, and dumps 80% in X. After estimation error, realized excess of X was noise — the ‘frontier’ portfolio was an estimation artifact, not a free lunch. If estimated E[r]_X=12% vs 8% for Y with similar vol/corr, optimizer piles into X. After noise, realized excess may be ~0 — the optimal weight was estimation error, not an edge.
eli5: A computer can draw a “best mix” chart from estimated guesses. If the guesses are noisy, the “perfect” mix can be a confident mistake.

title: Beta as co-movement
body: Beta measures sensitivity to a market factor, not standalone ‘riskiness.’ A low-beta name can still blow up idiosyncratically; a high-beta name can be a leveraged play on a factor everyone already owns. Know which risk you are being paid for. Beta is sensitivity to a chosen factor, not a moral measure of riskiness. Residual blow-ups and wrong-factor betas are why hedging the market can still leave large P&L.
example: Stock returns ≈ 1.5 × market moves in the estimation window (β ≈ 1.5). If the market is −10%, the linear beta story predicts ~−15% for the stock before alpha/residual. A −30% print means large idiosyncratic underperformance on top of beta. β=1.5 and market −10% ⇒ linear move ~−15%. Realized −30% ⇒ residual ≈ −15% beyond beta. Hedge ratios sized on beta alone miss that residual.
eli5: Beta asks how hard something moves when the whole market moves — like how much your boat rocks when the harbor swells — not whether the boat can still spring a unique leak.

title: Sharpe ratio limits
body: Sharpe ratio is excess return per unit of volatility. It assumes roughly symmetric, stable returns and ignores liquidity, leverage constraints, and tail shape. Selling crash insurance can inflate Sharpe until the crash — an old trap. Sharpe rewards smooth excess return per vol and is silent on liquidity, leverage, and left-tail shape. Strategies that harvest pennies in front of a steamroller print beautiful Sharpes until they do not.
example: Fund returns 10% with 10% vol; risk-free is 4% ⇒ Sharpe = (10−4)/10 = 0.6. Another fund returns 9% with 6% vol by shorting vol ⇒ Sharpe = 0.83 — until a −25% gap month that the ratio never priced. Sharpe=(10−4)/10=0.6. Vol-selling fund (9−4)/6=0.83 looks better until a −25% gap month — the ratio never encoded crash exposure or liquidity.
eli5: Sharpe is a neat score of extra reward per bumpiness. It can look great for strategies that are calm until a rare disaster — the score did not see the disaster.

title: Correlation ≠ causation in markets
body: Sample correlations are unstable across regimes. Assets that diversify in calm markets often co-crash when funding liquidity dries up. Treat historical correlation as a clue for stress design, not a contract with the future. Sample correlations are regime statistics, not structural constants. Design hedges and risk limits for the stressed co-movement you fear, not the calm-window average in the teaser deck.
example: Credit and equity show correlation 0.2 in a calm five-year window. In a funding panic both sell off together and realized correlation prints 0.8 for a quarter — destroying the diversification the calm sample promised. Calm ρ≈0.2 can print ρ≈0.8 in a funding panic. A risk model using 0.2 undersizes joint losses exactly when diversification is needed most.
eli5: Two things moving together in calm weather may crash together in a storm. Old “they don’t move together” charts can fail when everyone needs cash at once.

title: Bond duration
body: Macaulay duration is the weighted-average time to cash flows; modified duration approximates percentage price change for a yield move. Longer duration means more rate sensitivity — including more pain for ‘safe’ bonds when yields rise. Modified duration is a local linear map from yield to price; it fails for large moves and for bonds with material optionality. Key-rate durations matter when the curve does not shift in parallel.
example: Modified duration ≈ 7. A +100 bp parallel yield rise implies ≈ −7% price move (before convexity). On a $10m DV01-relevant book, that is roughly a $700k mark-to-market hit for a clean parallel shift. ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod×Δy = −7×0.01 = −7%. On $10m: about −$700k for a clean +100 bp parallel move before convexity and key-rate effects.
imageCredit: Diagram: Bond price–yield, duration vs convexity (Wikimedia Commons)
eli5: Duration is a sensitivity dial for a bond: a longer dial means prices move more when interest rates change — like a longer seesaw for the same push.

title: Convexity
body: Duration is a linear approximation; convexity captures curvature. For plain vanilla bonds, positive convexity means prices rise more (and fall less) than duration predicts for large yield moves — valuable, and usually not free in yield terms. Positive convexity is valuable asymmetry versus the duration tangent — and usually paid for in yield. Negative convexity (many callables/MBS) means you can be wrong on both the rate path and the hedge ratio.
example: Duration predicts −7% for +100 bp. With meaningful positive convexity, actual price drop might be ~−6.5% instead. For −100 bp, price might rise ~+7.5% rather than +7% — the asymmetry duration alone misses. Duration estimate −7% for +100 bp; with positive convexity, actual maybe ~−6.5%. For −100 bp, maybe ~+7.5% vs +7% linear — the asymmetry is the convexity P&L.
imageCredit: Diagram: Bond price–yield, duration vs convexity (Wikimedia Commons)
eli5: Convexity is the bend in the bond’s price path. Big rate jumps do not follow a perfectly straight line — the bend can soften hits and improve big gains.

title: Yield curve shapes
body: The yield curve embeds rate expectations, risk premia, and sometimes segmented demand. Inversion (short rates above long) has often preceded slowdowns, but it is a signal about the curve — not a timing oracle for equities or credit spreads. Curve shape mixes rate expectations, term premium, and segmented demand. Inversion is information about forwards and premia — not a stopwatch for equity sell-offs.
example: 2y yield 5.0%, 10y yield 4.2% ⇒ 2s10s = −80 bp (inverted). That says the curve prices lower forward short rates and/or term-premium effects — it does not by itself say ‘sell equities next month.’ 2s10s = 4.2% − 5.0% = −80 bp. That describes an inverted curve / lower forwards and/or term-premium effects — it is not by itself a timed equity signal.
imageCredit: Diagram: U.S. Treasury yield curve (Wikimedia Commons)
eli5: The yield curve is a lineup of interest rates for different waiting times. When short rates sit above long ones, it warns about the path of rates — not a stock-market calendar.

title: Credit spreads
body: A credit spread compensates for expected default loss, risk premia, and liquidity. Spread tightening is not always fundamentals improving — it can be a hunt for yield compressing risk compensation. Read spreads as a price of risk, not a moral score. Decompose spread into expected loss, risk premium, and liquidity. Tightening can be better fundamentals or simply cheaper risk compensation — those are different trades.
example: Corporate yield 6.5%, matched Treasury 4.0% ⇒ spread = 250 bp. body: Leverage amplifies gains and losses and shortens the time you can be wrong. The same return target with more leverage means thinner buffers against volatility, margin calls, and gap risk. body: Stress tests ask ‘what if’ under severe but plausible scenarios rather than average history. Good stresses break multiple assumptions at once (rates, spreads, liquidity, FX). body: OTC exposure is not just today’s mark — it is the risk your counterparty fails when the trade has positive replacement value. body: Ops risk covers process failures, cyber, fraud, and model misuse — losses without a market move. Crowding, definition drift, and implementation costs decide whether the academic premium survives live trading. Factors have economic stories and multi-year drawdowns. Crowding, definition drift, and costs decide whether the academic premium survives live.
example: Value factor backtest +3%/year. After costs, crowding, and a definition that drifted toward cheap low-quality names, live value sleeve prints +0.5% for a decade with a multi-year −20% relative drawdown — premium ≠ smooth annuity. Backtest +3%/yr can become +0.5% live after costs/crowding with a −20% relative multi-year drawdown — premium ≠ annuity.
eli5: Factor investing follows repeatable traits — like preferring cheaper or stronger-momentum names. The recipe can work over long stretches and still taste bad for years.

title: Regime shifts
body: Return and correlation statistics are regime-dependent. Strategies optimized on one volatility/correlation regime can fail in another. The expensive assumption in a risk model is ‘this time looks like the sample.’ Risk models estimated in one vol/correlation regime mis-size positions in another. The expensive assumption is that the sample looks like tomorrow.
example: Risk model estimated on 2010–2019 calm data. 2020 gap move prints 5σ under that covariance. Positions sized for the calm regime are suddenly oversized — the regime shift, not a single name, drove the blow-up. 2010–19 covariance marks a 2020 gap as many-σ. Positions sized for calm are suddenly oversized — regime, not one ticker, drove the blow-up.
eli5: Market weather changes: calm rules can fail in storm rules. A plan built only on sunny data can be the wrong size when the weather breaks.

title: Moral hazard in finance
body: When losses are shared with taxpayers or counterparties but gains are private, risk-taking expands. Prudential regulation, bail-in, and skin-in-the-game rules try to realign incentives — imperfectly, because crises rewrite rules in real time. When upside is private and downside is shared, risk-taking expands. Capital, bail-in, and skin-in-the-game rules try to realign incentives — imperfectly in crises.
example: Bank equity holders capture upside from leveraged risk; downside beyond equity is borne by creditors/taxpayers if resolution is incomplete. Expecting a backstop lowers the private cost of tail risk — classic moral hazard. Equity captures leveraged upside; losses beyond equity hit creditors/taxpayers if resolution is incomplete. Expected backstops lower private tail-cost — classic hazard.
eli5: If winners keep the candy and losers share the mess with others, people may take bigger risks. Good rules try to make risk-takers keep more of their own downside.

title: Netting and close-out
body: Master agreements allow close-out netting: on default, offset positive and negative contract values into one claim. That shrinks gross exposure dramatically — and makes legal enforceability of netting a systemic plumbing issue. Close-out netting collapses gross derivatives exposure into one claim on default. Legal enforceability of netting is systemic plumbing, not a legal nicety.
example: You are +$30m on Swap A and −$25m on Swap B with the same counterparty. Without netting, gross credit exposure concerns both. With close-out netting, claim ≈ +$5m net — $25m of gross disappears legally. +30 and −25 with same counterparty ⇒ net claim ~+5 with close-out netting vs worrying about both gross legs without it — $25m gross legally offsets.
eli5: Netting means adding up what you owe each other and keeping only the leftover. It can turn two big scary numbers into one smaller one when someone fails.

title: Haircuts and procyclicality
body: Collateral haircuts rise when volatility rises, demanding more capital exactly when marks are stressed. That procyclicality turns trade-level prudence into system-wide deleveraging pressure. Haircuts rise with volatility, demanding more capital exactly when marks hurt. Micro prudence becomes macro deleveraging pressure.
example: Haircut on corporate bonds 5% in calm markets, 15% in stress. A $100m portfolio that supported $95m financing suddenly supports $85m — forced $10m deleveraging into the same stress that widened haircuts. Haircut 5%→15% on $100m portfolio: financable amount 95→85 ⇒ $10m forced delever into the stress that widened haircuts.
eli5: A haircut is an extra safety cushion lenders demand on collateral. In scary times cushions grow — forcing more sales exactly when prices hurt.

title: LIBOR to SOFR transition
body: LIBOR was a panel-estimated interbank rate; SOFR is a transaction-based overnight Treasury repo rate. The transition rewired loan, derivative, and fallback conventions — a reminder that ‘the floating rate’ is an institutional construct. SOFR is transaction-based overnight repo; LIBOR was panel-estimated. Spread adjustments and fallback language change floating-rate economics by tens of bp.
example: A loan paying LIBOR+150 bp migrates to SOFR + a spread adjustment (~10–25 bp historically for some tenors) + margin. Two ‘floating’ loans can differ by tens of bp purely from benchmark and fallback choices. LIBOR+150 may become SOFR + spread adjustment (~10–25 bp historically for some tenors) + margin — two floating loans can differ by tens of bp from benchmark choice alone.
eli5: The old floating-rate benchmark was partly a survey; the newer one is built from real overnight trades. Switching benchmarks can quietly change the interest you pay.

title: Duration gap banking
body: Banks often fund longer-duration assets with shorter-duration liabilities. That maturity transformation earns spread in calm markets and can devastate economic value when rates reprice liabilities faster than assets. Funding long assets with shorter liabilities earns spread until liability costs reprice faster than assets. Economic value of equity is highly gap-sensitive.
example: Assets duration 5 years, liabilities duration 1 year, duration gap ≈ 4. Rates +200 bp ⇒ rough economic value of equity hit scales with gap × size. Deposit costs reprice quickly while fixed-rate assets lag — classic gap pain. Asset duration 5, liability duration 1 ⇒ gap ~4. +200 bp hurts economic equity roughly with gap × size; deposit costs reprice faster than fixed-rate assets.
eli5: Banks often lend for longer waits than the money customers can ask back quickly. That gap earns money in calm times and hurts when funding costs jump fast.

title: Liquidity coverage ratio idea
body: LCR-style rules require enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a modeled short stress outflow. They reduce run risk — and increase demand for the same safe assets everyone needs in a crisis. LCR-style HQLA requirements reduce run risk and concentrate demand for the same safe assets in system stress.
example: Modeled 30-day net outflows $10b ⇒ LCR needs ≥$10b HQLA if the ratio target is 100%. In system stress, many banks need the same HQLA at once — regulation reduces idiosyncratic run risk while concentrating demand for safe assets. $10b modeled 30-day outflows ⇒ ≥$10b HQLA at 100% LCR. System stress: many banks need the same HQLA simultaneously — safe-asset demand concentrates.
eli5: Rules ask banks to keep enough easy-to-sell safe assets for a short storm of withdrawals. Helpful for runs — and it makes everyone want the same safe stuff in a crisis.

title: Mark-to-market vs mark-to-model
body: Level 1 marks use observable prices; deeper levels rely more on models and unverifiable inputs. In stress, the boundary between ‘price’ and ‘model’ becomes a governance and capital question, not just an accounting footnote. Observable marks versus model marks is a governance and capital issue in stress. Reclassification to fire-sale comparables can gap capital overnight.
example: Liquid Treasury: Level 1 mark from screens. Complex tranche with no reliable print: Level 3 model mark. In a crisis, moving an asset from ‘model’ to a fire-sale comparable can gap capital overnight — classification mattered. Treasury: Level 1 screen. Complex tranche: Level 3 model. Crisis re-mark to fire-sale comparable can gap capital overnight — classification was capital.
eli5: Some prices come from clear screens; others come mostly from models. In a crisis, switching from a model guess to a panicked sale price can shock the numbers overnight.

title: Adverse selection in markets
body: Liquidity providers lose to informed traders and widen spreads or pull quotes to compensate. When information asymmetry spikes, markets can gap not because nobody knows the price, but because nobody wants to be the bid. When informed flow arrives, liquidity providers widen or pull — spreads are partly insurance against being picked off. Gaps can be defense, not only news about cash flows.
example: Ahead of a merger rumor, informed flow lifts the offer repeatedly. Market makers widen spreads from 2¢ to 20¢ or drop size. Observed ‘volatility’ is partly adverse-selection defense, not only news about cash flows. Informed flow lifts offers; MM widens 2¢→20¢ or pulls size. Measured vol partly reflects adverse-selection defense, not only cash-flow news.
eli5: If traders fear the other side knows more, they widen their prices or step back. Sometimes the market jumps because nobody wants to be the buyer, not because nobody has a guess.
